client: I just got my calculus final exam back, and I completely failed it. I've been questioning whether I'm even cut out for this engineering major. Everyone else seems to get it so easily, and I just feel stupid and inadequate.
therapist: It sounds like this exam result has really shaken your confidence and left you doubting your abilities. Let's take a moment to explore these thoughts—when you say "everyone else seems to get it so easily," what makes you feel that way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I feel that way because I see my classmates discussing the material like it’s nothing, while I’m struggling to even understand the basics. It makes me feel like I’m just not smart enough or that I’m falling behind everyone else. It’s hard not to compare myself when it seems so effortless for them.
therapist: It seems like this comparison to your classmates is really weighing on you, especially when you feel like you're struggling more than they are. It might help to explore what specific challenges you're facing with the material—what part of the basics feels the most difficult for you to grasp?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I feel like everyone else just gets it so easily, and I’m stuck trying to understand the basics. It’s frustrating because I spend so much time studying, but I still feel lost, especially with the foundational concepts. I worry that if I don’t catch up soon, I’ll just fall further behind.
therapist: It sounds like you're putting in a lot of effort but still feeling frustrated when the concepts don't click as quickly as you'd like. Let's explore this idea that you'll "fall further behind"—what would that look like to you, and how would you know if it were happening?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know exactly what falling further behind would look like, but I just have this constant dread that I'm not improving fast enough. Like everyone else is getting their lives together while I'm stuck in the same anxious thought patterns. It's frustrating because I am trying, but I still wake up with this heavy feeling every morning.
therapist: It sounds like this worry about falling behind is creating a lot of ongoing stress, especially when it feels like others are progressing more smoothly. Let’s focus on what you’re already doing—what steps have you taken so far to work through these challenges?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I’ve tried to keep up by making lists and setting goals, but it feels like I’m just spinning my wheels. Every time I check something off, there’s twice as much waiting. It’s exhausting, and I keep comparing myself to others who seem to have it all figured out. I don’t know if I’m even doing the right things to catch up.
therapist: It sounds like you're putting a lot of effort into staying organized, but it still feels overwhelming when the workload keeps piling up. When you compare yourself to others, what specific qualities or actions do you feel they have that you’re missing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I guess I feel like others just handle stress better than I do. They seem to stay calm and focused, even when things get chaotic, while I feel like I’m constantly on edge and struggling to keep up. It’s like they have this natural ability to manage time and prioritize, and I just don’t. 

But honestly, even talking about this makes me feel like I’m just making excuses for myself. Maybe I’m just not trying hard enough, or I’m not as capable as I think I should be. It’s frustrating because I want to do better, but it feels like I’m always falling short.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling overwhelmed by stress and self-doubt, especially when comparing yourself to others who seem to handle things more smoothly. Let’s explore this idea of trying harder—what would “trying harder” look like for you, and how would you know if it were enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: I don’t even know what “trying harder” would look like. Every time I push myself, I just end up exhausted and feeling like it’s still not good enough. Like last week, I stayed late every night to finish a project, but my coworker still got praised for doing less work. It’s so frustrating.
therapist: It sounds like you're putting in a lot of effort but still feeling unseen and undervalued, especially when others receive recognition for what feels like less work. Let’s explore what “good enough” would look like for you—how would you know if your efforts were truly meeting your own standards?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I don't even know what "good enough" would look like anymore. Every time I think I've met my own standards, I see someone else getting praised for doing less, and it makes me question everything. It's like my internal bar keeps moving higher no matter what I do. 

The idea of setting my own standards feels impossible when I'm constantly comparing myself to others. How can I trust my own judgment when external validation seems so random?
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a cycle where external comparisons keep shifting your sense of what "enough" looks like, making it hard to trust your own progress. Let's slow this down—when you notice yourself measuring your work against others' recognition, what happens to your ability to acknowledge your own effort?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I do compare myself to others a lot, especially at work. When I see someone getting praised or promoted, I immediately feel like I’m falling behind, even if I’ve been working hard. It’s like my effort doesn’t matter unless someone else notices it, and that makes me feel invisible. 

I try to acknowledge my own work, but it feels hollow because I don’t trust my own judgment. How can I know if I’m doing enough if no one else is saying so? It’s like I need external validation to feel like I’m on the right track. 

I guess slowing it down sounds good in theory, but it feels unnatural. When I’m in that moment of comparison, it’s hard to step back and think clearly. My mind just spirals, and I end up feeling worse about myself.
therapist: It sounds like this need for external validation is really intense—your words describe feeling stuck, but your voice carries a lot of urgency and frustration about it. When you notice that spiral starting, what’s the first sign that tells you you’re comparing yourself again?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know, maybe it's when my stomach drops after seeing someone's perfect life on Instagram? But sometimes I don't even notice I'm doing it until I'm already deep in that awful feeling. It's like my brain automatically measures my life against theirs before I can stop it. 

I guess I'm frustrated because I know it's irrational, but knowing that doesn't make the feeling go away. The more I try not to compare, the more I seem to do it.
therapist: It sounds like this comparison happens so quickly that it feels automatic, leaving you frustrated because even recognizing it doesn’t ease the emotional weight. Let’s try something different—next time you notice that stomach-drop moment, could you pause and name one thing you’re grateful for in your own life, even if it feels small?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
